newsitem.title: MOROCCO: FEATURE-Credit a luxury to most Moroccans.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Credit a luxury to most Moroccans.

text.p: Low incomes prevent most Moroccans from getting credit but there are still enough of them seeking it for rogue traders to see them as easy prey.
The government recently stepped in to lay down rules -- welcomed by responsible credit firms -- to protect people in a market which, despite limitations, is growing.
Credit firms today mostly turn away anyone earning below the national minimum wage of 1,700 dirhams ($184.7) a month.
"We should bear in mind that about 8.3 million of the population is active if you exclude children and women at home," Mostapha Melsa, general delegate at Morocco's credit firm association said.

He said an estimated 250,000 people out of a population of 27 million went to credit companies in 1995, the last year for which figures were available. But even this added up to a respectable figure of 4.283 billion dirhams ($357 million).
They sought money mainly for electrical appliances, furniture, motorcycles and cars.
"Credits are destined for modest people, excluded from banks because of their low salaries," he said.
INCREASE IN CREDIT GRANTED
The association calculated there was a 20 percent increase in the number of people getting credit in 1996 but he had no figure yet for the total amount granted.
According to Melsa, the banks have two million current accounts, of which more than 80 percent are empty for most of the month.

Those seeking credit wanted it for amounts ranging from 3,000 dirhams to 200,000 dirhams, repayable over a period up to 48 months. The average sum most often granted is between 7,000 and 15,000 dirhams -- enough to buy a television set, refrigerator, washing machine or motorcycle.
Recently the finance ministry and Central Bank signed a convention to draw up model credit agreements to prevent abuses which the media has denounced.

"Some people need the money so badly that they ask sellers to fill in an application to get the credit even if they will not buy anything. In return, the 'seller' demands a commission of 20 percent or more on the credit obtained," Melsa added.
Some of those seeking credit simply sign blank documents so the seller fills them as he wishes.
Melsa said "People tend to be trustful, they are usually busy; when the seller says 'just sign I'll cope with the procedures', they do".
FRAUD USED TO GET CREDIT

Another kind of cheating is when sellers xerox a document agreed by the finance ministry on rates and reimbursement periods. Some sellers manipulated lists, covering columns and changing others so as to extend the period of early higher repayment.
"We are devising a series of measures to stop these procedures. If the customer is honest, he will denounce the seller. If not, it means he is an accomplice," Melsa added.
Morocco has 32 consumers credit firms, whose interest rates can go up to 23 percent a year but terms vary according to length of time the credit is sought.
"The state will set soon a maximum interest rate to be respected by all firms," Melsa said.

It is now compulsory for credit firms to be part of a professional body and Melsa's association includes 65 firms of which 32 deal with consumer credit. The remainder handle industrial or other bigger loans.
BAD DEBTS AT 10 PERCENT OF CREDITS
Bad debts represent more than 10 percent of outstanding credits each year, Melsa said: "We always try to find an amicable solution. But if not we lodge a complaint with courts."
He termed credit "a blessing" for many, notably to avoid many workers having to borrow money from their company early in the month.
Melsa works with the Association Professionnelle des Societes de Financement, set up in 1994, one year after credit firms became liable to regulation of monetary authorities.

It aims to have its members respect legislation, improve banking techniques, stimulate competitiveness and act as an intermediary between members and authorities. Retailers not complying with rules governing credit will in future be blacklisted by all credit firms in the association.
The association also plans an education campaign, advising Moroccans on how they should go about obtaining credit.
"We will inform customers by mail of all the financing terms of their credit, even illiterate people have always in their circle an educated relative or friend".
More than half the population is illiterate.
